title: Notice of Claim Disallowance
description: A Notice of Claim Disallowance (IRS Letter 105C or 106C) is the IRS's final rejection of a refund claim and starts a two-year deadline to sue.
summary: A Notice of Claim Disallowance (IRS Letter 105C for a full denial or Letter 106C for a partial denial) is the IRS's final rejection of a U.S. refund claim, including R&D tax credits under IRC § 41. body.text: A Notice of Claim Disallowance (IRS Letter 105C for a full denial or Letter 106C for a partial denial) is the IRS's final rejection of a U.S. refund claim, including R&D tax credits under IRC § 41. Its certified mailing starts a two-year deadline under IRC § 6532(a)(1) to sue in federal court; Appeals review does not pause it.
Executive Summary and the Activation of the Statutory Clock

The Notice of Claim Disallowance (NOCD), formally issued by the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) as Letter 105C for a full denial or Letter 106C for a partial denial, constitutes the definitive administrative mechanism through which the United States federal government rejects a taxpayer's claim for a tax credit or refund. For corporate taxpayers claiming the Credit for Increasing Research Activities—commonly referred to as the Research and Development (R&D) tax credit under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) § 41—receipt of a Notice of Claim Disallowance immediately converts an administrative examination dispute into a jurisdictional legal controversy. Rather than functioning as an interim audit proposal or an invitation to continued informal dialogue, the notice operates as a final administrative determination that sets forth the specific factual and legal grounds for the adverse decision, records the formal date of determination, and identifies the exact tax periods affected. While the substantive basis for disallowance—ranging from technical ineligibility under statutory research criteria to inadequate forensic financial substantiation—remains central to the underlying controversy, the overriding legal consequence of the notice is strictly procedural: its mailing activates a rigid, non-extendable statutory clock governing access to the federal judiciary.

Upon the dispatch of Letter 105C or Letter 106C via certified or registered mail, IRC § 6532(a)(1) initiates a strict two-year (24-month) limitation period within which the claimant must file a formal refund lawsuit in either an appropriate United States District Court or the United States Court of Federal Claims. Because this two-year window is an explicit condition attached to the federal government's waiver of sovereign immunity, the deadline is strictly jurisdictional; the expiration of the 24-month period without a filed judicial complaint or a formally executed statutory extension permanently extinguishes the taxpayer's right to judicial review and forfeits the claimed credit revenue. Beneath the surface of individual audit disputes, this statutory design creates a profound asymmetry between administrative procedure and judicial jurisdiction: while the administrative apparatus encourages iterative document production and informal dispute resolution, the jurisdictional statute operates as an unforgiving bar that severs judicial remedies regardless of whether administrative discussions remain ongoing.

The financial and operational stakes in R&D tax credit controversies are particularly pronounced because corporate research claims routinely span multiple business units, involve complex multi-year engineering or software development expenditures, and face heightened IRS enforcement scrutiny over documentation traceability and statistical sampling methodologies. Furthermore, because the IRS utilizes the identical Letter 105C and Letter 106C procedural framework across diverse refund regimes—including both IRC § 41 research credits and pandemic-era claims such as the Employee Retention Credit (ERC)—the procedural hazard is standardized across federal tax administration. The widespread issuance of disallowance notices across high-volume refund programs has heightened institutional bottlenecks within the IRS, increasing the likelihood that post-disallowance administrative correspondence will languish beyond the two-year litigation window. Consequently, tax controversy counsel and corporate tax directors must prioritize compliance with the two-year judicial limitation period above ongoing administrative dialogue, regardless of the perceived technical strength of the underlying research activities.
Formal Designation and Administrative Architecture of the Notice of Claim Disallowance
Statutory Prerequisites and Required Notice Elements

Within the statutory architecture of federal tax procedure, the Notice of Claim Disallowance serves as the mandatory administrative bridge that a claimant must cross prior to invoking federal court jurisdiction. Under IRC § 6532(a)(1), a taxpayer is statutorily prohibited from instituting a refund suit unless the Secretary of the Treasury has either formally disallowed the claim or failed to render a decision for a minimum of six months from the date the claim was filed. This dual timing structure serves two distinct systemic functions: the six-month waiting period affords the IRS an initial window of administrative exclusivity to audit and process refund claims without premature judicial interference, whereas the issuance of a formal disallowance notice shifts the burden back to the taxpayer to either accept the adverse determination or escalate the controversy to an Article III or Article I federal refund forum within two years.

In the context of retrospective R&D tax credit claims, the administrative lifecycle typically begins when a taxpayer files an amended individual income tax return on Form 1040-X or an amended corporate income tax return on Form 1120-X seeking a refund or credit for prior tax years. Following submission, the IRS examination team conducts an audit, issuing Information Document Requests (IDRs) to verify Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) and Qualified Research Activities. If the examination team proposes to reject the claim in whole or in part, it issues a preliminary 30-day letter—such as Letter 566—granting the taxpayer 30 days to submit a formal written protest to the IRS Independent Office of Appeals. When the examination concludes without agreement and the taxpayer either bypasses the protest stage or fails to overturn the examination team's adverse findings during an Appeals conference, the IRS issues Letter 105C (full disallowance) or Letter 106C (partial disallowance) to formally close administrative processing of the claim.

To function as a legally valid notice that triggers the statutory limitation period under IRC § 6532(a)(1), Letter 105C or Letter 106C must communicate several essential data points to the claimant. Specifically, the notice must unequivocally state that the claimed refund or credit has been disallowed, articulate the specific factual or legal reason for the adverse IRS decision, record the exact date on which the decision was made, and identify the affected tax year or accounting period. Crucially, the letter must also notify the taxpayer of the two-year statutory window within which a judicial complaint must be filed to contest the disallowance in federal court. Because the two-year limitation period is measured directly from the date the notice is dispatched via certified or registered mail rather than the date the taxpayer receives or opens the correspondence, verifying the structural integrity of the notice and preserving the physical mailing envelope alongside the dated letter are foundational tasks in establishing the exact jurisdictional bar date. Any ambiguity between the date printed on the face of Letter 105C or Letter 106C and the postmark recorded on the certified mailing receipt must be resolved conservatively in favor of the earlier date to prevent inadvertent jurisdictional forfeiture.
Procedural Untimeliness Versus Substantive Merits Disallowance

The strategic trajectory of a post-NOCD controversy depends heavily upon whether the IRS bases its disallowance on a threshold procedural defect or a substantive disagreement on the technical and accounting merits. The most severe procedural ground for disallowance is original filing untimeliness under IRC § 6511. Pursuant to IRC § 6511 and administrative guidance set forth in IRS Publication 556, a taxpayer must generally file a claim for credit or refund within the later of three years from the date the original tax return was filed or two years from the date the tax was paid. When the IRS issues a Notice of Claim Disallowance on the ground that the underlying amended return or refund claim was submitted outside the IRC § 6511 window, the dispute is governed by IRC § 6514(a), which mandates that any refund of tax made after the expiration of the period of limitation for filing a claim is erroneous and any credit allowed after such period is legally void. In such procedural denials, substantive arguments regarding the scientific or technological merits of the taxpayer's R&D activities are rendered legally irrelevant unless the taxpayer can first establish through documentary mailing records or payment transcripts that the original refund claim was timely filed.

Conversely, when a Notice of Claim Disallowance is predicated on substantive grounds, the IRS challenges either the technical eligibility of the underlying research activities or the accounting substantiation of the claimed costs. Under IRC § 41, a taxpayer must demonstrate that its claimed activities satisfy the statutory four-part test—specifically proving that Qualified Research Expenses were incurred in attempting to eliminate technical uncertainty concerning the capability, method, or appropriate design of a business component through a rigorous process of experimentation. Substantive disallowances in R&D examinations predominantly arise from perceived documentation insufficiency, where the IRS asserts that the claimant failed to substantiate the nexus between financial expenditures and qualified research projects. Unlike a procedural untimeliness denial under IRC § 6511 and § 6514(a), which erects an absolute statutory bar at the threshold of the claim, a substantive disallowance leaves the door to federal court review fully open on a de novo evidentiary basis, shifting the taxpayer's burden toward compiling comprehensive project records, forensic accounting reconciliations, and expert technical testimony before the two-year judicial deadline expires.

body.text: Jurisdictional Mechanics of Internal Revenue Code Section 6532
The Two-Year Judicial Limitation Period and Forum Prerequisites

The procedural urgency surrounding Letter 105C and Letter 106C stems directly from the statutory mandate of IRC § 6532(a)(1), which establishes a rigid two-year period of limitation for commencing a tax refund suit measured from the date the Notice of Claim Disallowance is mailed by certified or registered mail. In federal tax litigation, this two-year timeframe is not a flexible administrative guideline subject to equitable tolling or excusable neglect; rather, it operates as an absolute condition of the sovereign immunity waiver of the United States and is strictly jurisdictional. If a claimant fails to file a formal complaint in either the appropriate United States District Court or the United States Court of Federal Claims on or before the two-year anniversary of the mailing date, the court lacks subject-matter jurisdiction and must dismiss the action automatically.

Furthermore, litigating a disallowed refund claim under IRC § 6532 differs fundamentally from contesting a proposed tax deficiency in the United States Tax Court. Whereas the U.S. Tax Court exercises prepayment deficiency jurisdiction triggered by a statutory Notice of Deficiency, refund suits brought in a U.S. District Court or the U.S. Court of Federal Claims are governed by the full-payment rule established in Flora v. United States (the Flora rule), which generally requires the taxpayer to have paid the disputed tax liability in full as a prerequisite to invoking judicial jurisdiction. Because the U.S. Tax Court lacks standalone jurisdiction to adjudicate refund suits following a Notice of Claim Disallowance absent an accompanying deficiency determination, taxpayers challenging an R&D credit disallowance on an amended return are restricted to the two federal refund forums. This forum restriction carries significant second-order implications for litigation strategy: counsel must not only satisfy the strict 24-month filing deadline, but must also evaluate differences in local circuit precedent, discovery scope, jury availability in U.S. District Court versus bench trials in the U.S. Court of Federal Claims, and the involvement of the Department of Justice Tax Division, which assumes defense of the government once a refund complaint is filed.
The Appeal Trap Under Section 6532(a)(4)

A frequent and catastrophic procedural hazard in post-disallowance tax controversy is the "Appeal Trap" codified in IRC § 6532(a)(4). Under this statutory provision, any administrative consideration, reconsideration, or action taken by the Secretary of the Treasury following the mailing of a Notice of Claim Disallowance by certified or registered mail does not extend, pause, or toll the two-year period within which a refund suit must be commenced. In practice, Letters 105C and 106C routinely contain standardized language explaining how a taxpayer may submit additional information to the IRS for reconsideration or request an administrative hearing before the IRS Independent Office of Appeals. Corporate taxpayers and general accounting practitioners frequently misinterpret this explicit administrative invitation to submit supplemental documentation or engage in Appeals conferences as an automatic administrative stay of the judicial clock.

Because IRC § 6532(a)(4) renders post-notice administrative action legally irrelevant to the running of the statute of limitations, an ongoing review by the Independent Office of Appeals provides zero legal protection against the expiration of the two-year deadline. This statutory divergence between administrative correspondence and jurisdictional law creates a severe behavioral trap: the more constructively an IRS examiner or Appeals officer engages with a taxpayer's supplemental R&D workpapers after Letter 105C is mailed, the more likely an unrepresented or misadvised claimant is to delay litigation past the 24-month cutoff. Even if an Appeals officer actively requests voluminous R&D substantiation records or engages in substantive settlement negotiations, the IRS is under no legal obligation to resolve the administrative appeal before the 24-month period lapses, and the agency must legally cease consideration and deny relief once the judicial bar date passes because any subsequent refund would be barred as erroneous under IRC § 6514(a). To neutralize this hazard, R&D controversy counsel must implement a mandatory dual-track defense strategy: while administrative reconsideration or Appeals engagement may be pursued as a cost-effective settlement channel, full litigation preparation must proceed simultaneously so that a protective refund complaint can be filed before the statutory deadline expires.
Statutory Extension via Form 907

Because informal administrative negotiations and post-disallowance Appeals submissions cannot pause the statutory clock under IRC § 6532(a)(4), the Internal Revenue Code provides only one valid legal mechanism to extend the deadline for bringing a refund suit. Under IRC § 6532(a)(2), the two-year limitation period may be extended exclusively through a formal, written stipulation executed by both the taxpayer and the IRS on Form 907 (Agreement to Extend the Time to Bring Suit). To be legally effective, Form 907 must be negotiated, approved, and physically or electronically signed by both the claimant and an authorized IRS official prior to the expiration of the original two-year limitation period. Unilateral submission of a signed Form 907 by the taxpayer without countersignature by an authorized IRS delegate before the 24-month anniversary confers no legal extension.

Crucially, the IRS exercises purely discretionary authority over whether to enter into a Form 907 extension and will not execute the agreement automatically upon request. According to Taxpayer Advocate Service guidance, the IRS generally agrees to sign Form 907 in specific, limited operational circumstances: when the agency requires additional time to complete internal administrative processing of the claim, when internal IRS routing or processing failures have adversely impacted the taxpayer (such as an administrative file being lost between IRS examination and Appeals functions), or when the Taxpayer Advocate Service (TAS) is actively engaged in resolving the taxpayer's case. Because internal IRS routing delays require time to obtain supervisory signatures on Form 907 itself, waiting until the final weeks of the 24-month window to request a statutory extension is operationally perilous. If the IRS declines to execute Form 907—or fails to return a fully countersigned copy—while an administrative appeal remains pending, counsel must treat the absence of a bilateral Form 907 as a definitive signal that administrative review will not preserve the claim, requiring immediate filing of a protective refund lawsuit in federal court.

body.text: Substantiation Burdens and Forensic Accounting Disputes in Research Credit Examinations
Statistical Sampling Failures and Population Refinement Deficits

Within the U.S. federal tax system, the R&D tax credit under IRC § 41 imposes an exceptionally rigorous substantiation standard. Because large corporate claimants frequently incur research expenditures across thousands of employees, multiple subsidiaries, and hundreds of cost centers, taxpayers routinely rely on statistical sampling methodologies to estimate and extrapolate total Qualified Research Expenses from a broader population of employee wages, supply costs, and contract research expenditures. Consequently, when IRS examiners—supported by internal IRS Subject Matter Experts (SMEs) and statistical specialists—disallow R&D claims via Letter 105C or Letter 106C, the controversy frequently centers not on abstract interpretations of statutory tax law, but on forensic accounting and statistical replicability failures.

As documented in the IRS Research Tax Credits Report Writing Pro Forma, examiners are instructed to issue a Notice of Claim Disallowance when deficiencies in the taxpayer's records prevent the Service from independently replicating or recreating the estimated QRE sample. In practice, four recurring methodological failures regularly trigger full disallowance of sampled R&D credit claims. First, population refinement deficits arise when the claimant fails to furnish all underlying reports, database queries, and electronic computer files utilized during the initial population refinement process that defined the sampling frame. When a taxpayer filters out cost centers or job titles prior to drawing a sample without preserving the exact digital audit trail of those exclusions, IRS statistical specialists cannot verify whether the resulting sampling frame is representative or biased. Second, financial book reconciliation failures occur when the claimant cannot reconcile the claimed QRE figures back to the corporation's underlying audited financial books and tax accounting records. Without a verifiable bridge between general ledger payroll accounts, Form W-2 wage totals, and the base population subjected to sampling, the entire claim lacks an auditable financial anchor.

Third, audit trails break down when the claimant fails to provide a formal written explanation accounting for missing documentation associated with specific selected sample units. In statistical sampling, an undocumented sample unit cannot simply be discarded or replaced with another project without destroying the random probability structure of the sample; failure to account for missing sample units invalidates the confidence interval of the estimate. Fourth, statistical validity collapses when the claimant lacks a justifiable mathematical or statistical basis for applying re-scaling factors when projecting sample results to the extrapolated QRE dollar total. When any combination of these four defects prevents the IRS examination team from verifying the mathematical integrity of the extrapolation, the examiner is empowered to treat the entire QRE computation as arbitrary and issue a Notice of Claim Disallowance rejecting the claimed credit in full. This administrative reality demonstrates a critical structural dynamic: modern R&D tax controversy operates at the intersection of tax law and forensic data governance, where the inability to reproduce digital audit trails and sampling frames is fatal at the administrative level regardless of the underlying scientific innovation.
Professional Liability and Recourse Against Negligent Advisors

When a Notice of Claim Disallowance is issued due to systemic substantiation failures—particularly where a third-party specialist firm engineered a flawed statistical sampling model or prepared retrospective claims lacking contemporaneous documentary support—the disallowance may generate a secondary legal cause of action for professional negligence. Corporate taxpayers frequently engage boutique R&D tax advisory consultancies or accounting firms on a contingent-fee or fixed-fee basis to identify eligible projects, conduct retrospective employee interviews, and compute QRE extrapolations. If an advisor's negligent preparation, departure from IRS statistical sampling standards, or misrepresentation of IRS substantiation requirements directly causes the IRS challenge and subsequent disallowance, the taxpayer may possess viable grounds to pursue professional liability damages against the advisor.

While a professional negligence action against a tax advisor cannot restore a forfeited federal tax refund from the U.S. Treasury if the underlying activities were ineligible or if the IRC § 6532 deadline was missed, civil recourse against a negligent advisor enables the corporate claimant to seek recovery of IRS-imposed accuracy-related penalties, statutory interest charges, and wasted professional and litigation fees that would have been avoided through competent tax counsel. Furthermore, where an advisor fails to warn the client of the two-year jurisdictional deadline triggered by Letter 105C or erroneously advises the client that post-disallowance Appeals reconsideration tolls the statute of limitations under IRC § 6532(a)(4), the advisor's malpractice directly causes the extinguishment of a potentially meritorious judicial claim. Consequently, immediately upon receipt of Letter 105C or Letter 106C, corporate legal counsel should institute a formal litigation hold to preserve not only internal R&D project records, but also all engagement letters, marketing representations, sampling workpapers, and electronic correspondence demonstrating the third-party advisor's methodology and procedural guidance.
Strategic Response Matrix and Hypothetical Case Analysis
Immediate Triage and Administrative Record Recovery

Receipt of a Notice of Claim Disallowance requires an immediate, disciplined triage protocol designed to protect jurisdictional deadlines while diagnosing the exact evidentiary posture of the dispute. First, controversy counsel must verify the exact certified or registered mailing date printed on Letter 105C or Letter 106C and archive the physical mailing envelope, as this date establishes the binding two-year statutory bar under IRC § 6532(a)(1). Second, counsel must confirm that the original amended return (Form 1040-X or Form 1120-X) satisfied the timeliness requirements of IRC § 6511 so that the claim is not barred at the threshold as an erroneous refund under IRC § 6514(a). Third, to clarify the precise factual and methodological grounds for the rejection, the taxpayer should immediately request the complete administrative examination file—including the examination team's workpapers, Subject Matter Expert reports, and statistical review memoranda—either directly from the IRS or through a formal Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request. Examining the internal IRS workpapers reveals whether the disallowance rests on remediable documentation gaps, specific sample replication errors under the IRS Research Tax Credits Report Writing Pro Forma, or fundamental legal disagreements regarding IRC § 41 eligibility.
Evaluation of Strategic Pathways and the TechNovation Inc. Hypothetical Model

Once the administrative file and jurisdictional dates are verified, the claimant must evaluate three strategic response tracks against the economic scale of the disputed credit. Under the first track, the taxpayer may elect to agree and accept the disallowance. If internal triage reveals an irrefutable jurisdictional flaw—such as an untimely original claim under IRC § 6511—or if the substantiation deficit is so severe that reconstructing the forensic accounting record is impossible or prohibitively expensive relative to the credit amount, conceding the disallowance prevents the expenditure of unrecoverable litigation costs. Under the second track, if the disallowance stems from discrete documentation gaps that can be cured through supplemental reconciliations or technical narratives, the taxpayer may pursue administrative reconsideration or review by the IRS Independent Office of Appeals. However, because IRC § 6532(a)(4) prevents Appeals review from tolling the two-year statute, this second pathway is viable only if the taxpayer simultaneously negotiates and executes Form 907 under IRC § 6532(a)(2) or maintains strict readiness to file suit prior to the 24-month deadline. Under the third track, for high-value R&D claims or disputes where the IRS refuses to sign Form 907, the taxpayer must pursue federal refund litigation by bypassing prolonged administrative reconsideration—or terminating it prior to the bar date—and filing a formal refund complaint in a U.S. District Court or the U.S. Court of Federal Claims before the IRC § 6532(a)(1) period expires.

To illustrate how these statutory rules and financial trade-offs interact in practice, consider the hypothetical case study of TechNovation Inc. TechNovation Inc., a software development corporation, identifies $150,000 in previously unclaimed R&D tax credits under IRC § 41 for software engineering activities conducted three years earlier and files an amended corporate income tax return on Form 1120-X to claim the refund. During the subsequent IRS examination, the audit team concludes that TechNovation's internal employee time-tracking records are too vague to substantiate the nexus between employee wages and qualified research activities. Following an unsuccessful protest to the Independent Office of Appeals, the IRS mails Letter 105C (Notice of Claim Disallowance) via certified mail on March 1, 2024.

In the TechNovation Inc. calculation, the mailing of Letter 105C on March 1, 2024 establishes an absolute statutory deadline of March 1, 2026 (24 months) under IRC § 6532(a)(1). Evaluating the financial and procedural parameters step by step reveals severe operational constraints for middle-market refund claims. Against a gross claimed benefit of $150,000 in IRC § 41 R&D tax credits claimed via Form 1120-X, prosecuting a federal refund action in U.S. District Court or the U.S. Court of Federal Claims requires an estimated litigation expenditure of $50,000 in external legal fees. Assuming full vindication on the merits in federal court, the maximum net economic recovery is computed as:
Maximum Net Recovery = $150,000 − $50,000 = $100,000
This yields a maximum net recovery ratio of:
Net Recovery Ratio = $100,000 ÷ $150,000 = 66.67%

Thus, even before factoring in litigation hazards, expert witness fees, or partial settlement concessions, transaction costs consume one-third (33.33%) of the gross credit value. This economic threshold creates a structural enforcement dynamic: for smaller or middle-market R&D claims where fixed federal litigation costs represent a high proportion of the claimed refund, the issuance of Letter 105C imposes an immediate financial barrier to judicial review, making administrative resolution via a timely Form 907 extension economically vital. Conversely, if TechNovation attempts to avoid the $50,000 litigation cost by submitting supplemental time-tracking records to the IRS for administrative reconsideration without obtaining an executed Form 907 and waits until March 2, 2026—just one day after the 24-month window expires—to file its judicial complaint, IRC § 6532(a)(1) and § 6532(a)(4) mandate automatic dismissal of the lawsuit for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, reducing the recoverable value from $100,000 to $0.

body.text: Preventative Audit Controls and Systemic Legislative Reform
Internal Traceability and Perpetual Litigation Readiness

Mitigating the legal and financial exposure associated with a Notice of Claim Disallowance requires corporate taxpayers to implement two complementary operational standards: preventative internal audit controls during claim preparation and perpetual litigation readiness upon claim submission. Because IRS disallowances of R&D tax credits predominantly target accounting methodology and sample replicability rather than pure statutory interpretation, internal corporate controls must be engineered from the outset so that an IRS examiner and statistical specialist can independently "recreate the sample" during an examination.

Specifically, effective preventative governance rests on three structural pillars integrated directly into the taxpayer's accounting and engineering workflow. First, corporations must deploy financial traceability systems—including project-accounting and time-tracking architectures—that directly tag Qualified Research Expenses, particularly employee wage allocations and supply expenditures, to discrete, documented research projects supported by project calendars and general ledger reconciliations. Second, when statistical sampling is utilized to extrapolate QREs across large corporate populations, the sampling frame, population refinement files, database queries, and re-scaling factors must undergo independent statistical validation by a qualified statistical specialist prior to filing to ensure full compliance with the IRS Research Tax Credits Report Writing Pro Forma. Preserving a locked, immutable archive of all population refinement scripts and sample unit documentation at the time the return is filed eliminates the primary forensic triggers for Letter 105C and Letter 106C disallowances. Third, taxpayers must enforce contemporaneous documentation capture rather than relying on retrospective reconstruction studies conducted years after the tax period closes, ensuring that technical narratives, hypotheses, and experimentation logs are recorded concurrently with the underlying engineering or software development activities.

Once an R&D claim receives a Notice of Claim Disallowance via Letter 105C or Letter 106C, the taxpayer must immediately transition from audit defense to perpetual litigation readiness. Under this standard, controversy counsel is engaged immediately upon receipt of the notice to preserve evidence, verify the certified mailing postmark, evaluate venue options between the U.S. District Court and the U.S. Court of Federal Claims, and draft a formal judicial complaint well in advance of the 24-month bar date. Administrative channels such as post-disallowance Appeals reconsideration are utilized strictly as bounded settlement leverage while counsel either secures a countersigned Form 907 extension well ahead of the expiration date or files a timely protective refund suit.
Legislative Tolling Proposals for Independent Office of Appeals Reviews

Beyond taxpayer-level compliance, the procedural architecture of IRC § 6532 highlights a systemic inefficiency in federal tax administration that warrants targeted legislative reform. Under the current text of IRC § 6532(a)(4), the absolute refusal to toll the two-year judicial limitation period during post-disallowance administrative reconsideration forces taxpayers into a counterproductive dilemma: claimants who are actively and constructively negotiating with the IRS Independent Office of Appeals following the issuance of Letter 105C or Letter 106C must either obtain discretionary IRS approval on Form 907 or incur substantial legal expenses—such as the $50,000 litigation cost illustrated in the TechNovation Inc. model—solely to file a protective federal lawsuit that preserves their statutory rights.

Forcing taxpayers and the Department of Justice to initiate federal court litigation while administrative settlement discussions remain unfinished undermines the statutory dispute-resolution mandate of the Independent Office of Appeals, penalizes middle-market claimants whose claims cannot absorb premature litigation fees, and burdens federal judicial dockets with protective complaints. Furthermore, the current regime disproportionately harms unrepresented or misadvised taxpayers who rely in good faith on the reconsideration instructions printed on Letters 105C and 106C, only to discover after 24 months that their ongoing administrative dialogue failed to pause the jurisdictional clock. A targeted legislative remedy would amend IRC § 6532 to formally toll and suspend the running of the two-year statute of limitations during the pendency of a formal, timely submitted review before the IRS Independent Office of Appeals. Aligning the statutory limitation clock with active Appeals jurisdiction would eliminate the involuntary forfeiture of judicial rights caused by the Section 6532(a)(4) Appeal Trap, reduce unnecessary protective litigation expenses for both taxpayers and the government, and promote efficient administrative resolution of complex R&D tax credit controversies.
